brief.topic: How a Third Filter Lets Light Through

s01: Two crossed polarizing filters can block the light.
Place another filter between them, at an angle.
Some light returns.
Nothing has created new light.
The middle filter changes which component can continue.
These are front views of three successive filters.
Their lines mark the directions they transmit.
After the first filter, the light is vertically polarized.
Call its intensity one.
The last filter transmits the horizontal component.
A vertical vibration has no horizontal component.
So without the middle filter, the output is zero.
Now look at the slanted direction in between.
An ideal filter keeps the projection onto its own axis.
The vertical field has a component along that diagonal.
The diagonal field has a horizontal component in turn.
Two smaller projections can survive where one cannot.
At forty five degrees, each projection multiplies the field
by the cosine of forty five degrees.
Intensity is proportional to the square of the field.
So each of these two filters passes half its incoming intensity.
One becomes one half, then one quarter.
Those fractions start after the first filter.
Turn the middle axis toward either outside axis.
The final light fades again.
The largest output is halfway between, at forty five degrees.
Real filters absorb additional light and leak a little.
This is the ideal projection model, called Malus law.
Sometimes a path appears when we allow an intermediate direction.
